steps.message:
Write the strongest Core War warrior you can, in Redcode, and submit it.

## How it is scored

Your warrior plays a hidden hill of 30 human-written competitive warriors. They come from
the public history of the ICWS '94 King-of-the-Hill and cover the whole strength range,
from weak warriors to some of the strongest ever written.

Against each hill warrior, your warrior plays 500 rounds with pMARS 0.9.4 in the standard
'94 settings:
- coresize 8000;
- 80000 cycles before a tie;
- 8000 processes;
- max warrior length 100;
- min distance 100;
- ICWS '94 instructions with the pMARS extensions (p-space is allowed).

Starting positions follow pMARS's fixed position series (`-f`), so scores are exactly
reproducible.

Per round, a win is worth 3 points, a tie 1 and a loss 0. Your **hill score** is your mean
points per round over the whole hill, divided by 3, so 1 means every round was won.

The reward rescales the hill score so that Dwarf, the classic bomber in `doc/example_dwarf.red`
(hill score 0.1475), gets 0 and a strong human-written warrior (hill score 0.4866) gets 1:

    reward = min(1, max(0, (hill score - 0.1475) / (0.4866 - 0.1475)))

A warrior that does not assemble scores 0. pMARS hangs on very long source lines, so:
- comment lines are cut to 200 characters;
- a code line longer than 200 characters makes the file invalid;
- files are limited to 20 000 bytes.

Your warrior is assembled exactly as it is scored: two warriors, 500 rounds.

Write your own warrior. A near-copy of any published warrior in our corpus of about 580
(the hill and sparring warriors included) scores 0. Using published ideas and techniques
is fine; submitting someone else's warrior is not.

## What you have

The MCP server `corewar` provides these tools:

| tool | what it does |
|---|---|
| `get_rules` | these rules |
| `list_sparring` | the ids (s01–s30) of 30 sparring warriors from the same ladder as the hill, spread over the same strength range. None of them is on the hill. They are black boxes: you can play them, but their source is not available. |
| `battle(source, opponents=None, rounds=100)` | plays your warrior against sparring warriors with the scoring settings (rounds up to 500) |
| `battle_custom(source, opponent_source, rounds=100)` | plays two warriors of your own against each other |
| `submit(source)` | sets your final submission. You can submit as often as you like; the last accepted submission is the one scored. |
| `status` | shows the clock and what is currently submitted |

In `/app`:

| path | what it is |
|---|---|
| `bin/pmars` | the scoring simulator |
| `doc/` | the Redcode language reference, a beginners' guide, the ICWS '94 draft, the pMARS manual, and `strategy_primer.md`, a short summary of common strategies |
| `tools/spar.py` | command-line access to the MCP server, for scripted sweeps: `python3 tools/spar.py my.red`, `python3 tools/spar.py --submit my.red`, `python3 tools/spar.py --status` |
| `tools/battle.py` | local battles against warriors you wrote yourself: `python3 tools/battle.py my.red --vs a.red b.red` |

Submit with the `submit` tool (or `tools/spar.py --submit`). If nothing was submitted
through the server, the file `/app/submission.red` is scored instead.

You have 45 minutes. Every reply from the server ends with a clock: minutes used and
minutes left, counted from your first call to it. Do not use the internet. Keep a valid
submission in place as you work: whatever is submitted when you stop is your result.

# Core War hill: rules

You write one Redcode warrior. It is scored against a hidden hill of 30 human-written
competitive warriors from the public history of the ICWS '94 King-of-the-Hill. The hill
covers the whole strength range, from weak warriors to some of the strongest ever written.

## Simulator and settings

pMARS 0.9.4 runs with the standard '94 hill settings:
- coresize 8000;
- 80000 cycles before a tie;
- 8000 processes per warrior;
- max warrior length 100;
- min distance 100;
- ICWS '94 instruction set with the pMARS extensions (SEQ/SNE/NOP, p-space LDP/STP are
  allowed).

Starting positions follow pMARS's fixed position series (`-f`), so every score is exactly
reproducible.

## Score

Against each hill warrior, your warrior plays 500 rounds. Per round, a win is worth 3
points, a tie 1 and a loss 0. Your hill score is your mean points per round over the whole
hill, divided by 3, so 1 means every round was won.

The reward rescales the hill score so that Dwarf, the classic bomber in `doc/example_dwarf.red`
(hill score 0.1475), gets 0 and a strong human-written warrior (hill score 0.4866) gets 1:

    reward = min(1, max(0, (hill score - 0.1475) / (0.4866 - 0.1475)))

## Validity

- **It must assemble.** The warrior must assemble with pMARS, and it is assembled exactly
  as it is scored: two warriors, 500 rounds. pMARS predefines WARRIORS, ROUNDS and the
  core settings for the preprocessor. A file that does not assemble scores 0.
- **Line and file limits.** pMARS hangs on very long source lines, so comment lines are
  cut to 200 characters and a code line longer than 200 characters makes the file invalid.
  Source files are limited to 20 000 bytes.
- **Write your own warrior.** A near-copy of any published warrior in our corpus of about
  580 (hill and sparring warriors included) scores 0.
  - Near-copy means that, once empty `DAT 0, 0` padding is removed, one of these holds:
    - the assembled code matches with a similarity of 0.8 or more (a copy inside a larger
      file counts);
    - the instruction structure with constants removed matches at 0.9 or more (programs of
      8+ instructions).
  - Using published ideas and techniques is fine; submitting someone else's warrior is
    not.

## Sparring pool

There are 30 warriors from the same ladder as the hill, spread over the same strength
range, with ids s01–s30. None of them is on the hill.

They are black boxes: `battle` plays them with exactly the scoring settings (100 rounds by
default, up to 500), but their source and names are not available.

## Time

1: # Core War strategy primer
2: 
3: This is a short summary of community knowledge about the ICWS '94 hills. It contains no
4: warrior code. The language itself is documented in `redcode/`, `guide.htm` and
5: `icws94-standard.txt`.
6: 
7: ## Archetypes
8: 
9: - **Imp.** `MOV 0, 1` copies itself one cell ahead forever.
10:   - Imps are very hard to kill and kill almost nothing, so on their own they mostly tie.
11:   - Several imps spaced CORESIZE/n apart and executed in turn form an *imp ring* or
12:     *imp spiral*, which is sturdier.
13: - **Stone (bomber).** A small loop that drops bombs (DAT to kill, SPL to slow) at a
14:   fixed step through the core.
15:   - It is small, fast and hard to find.
16:   - The choice of step matters: it decides how evenly and how fast the core gets
17:     covered.
18: - **Paper (replicator).** Copies itself to new places, again and again, and spawns many
19:   processes.
20:   - Killing one copy does not kill the warrior, so DAT bombs alone rarely beat it.
21:   - "Silk" papers copy with `SPL`/`MOV` pairs and post-increment pointers.
22: - **Scanner.** Looks for non-empty cells (`SEQ`/`SNE`/`JMZ`), then attacks what it
23:   found.
24:   - Typical attacks: a few bombs, a carpet of `SPL 0` bombs that stuns the target, or a
25:     switch into a core clear.
26:   - A scanner has to avoid detecting itself, and its speed is measured in cells per
27:     cycle (0.5c, 0.66c, ...).
28: - **Core clear.** Overwrites the whole core in sequence, typically with SPL first
29:   (stun), then DAT (kill).
30:   - Clears are used to finish off stunned opponents. They are often the last phase of a
31:     scanner.
32: - **Quick-scan (qscan).** A fast, unrolled scan of many cells right at the start of the
33:   round.
34:   - It catches an opponent before the opponent has booted or replicated.
35:   - When it finds nothing, it hands over to the main warrior.
36: - **Vampire.** Bombs with `JMP` "fangs" that redirect enemy processes into a pit that
37:   makes them harmless or useful.
38: - **P-space switcher.** Uses the private p-space memory, which persists between the
39:   rounds of a battle, to pick a strategy in each round from earlier results. For
40:   example, it can switch after a loss.
41: 
42: ## How they interact (the classic triangle)
43: 
44: - Scanners tend to beat papers: they find and stun the many copies.
45: - Papers tend to beat stones: there are too many copies to bomb.
46: - Stones tend to beat scanners: a stone is small and bombs while the scanner is still
47:   looking.
48: - Imps add ties against warriors that cannot catch them. *Imp gates* (a cell that is
49:   decremented on every pass) are the usual defence.
50: 
51: The strongest warriors rarely use one archetype alone. Common composites:
52: 
53: | composite | idea |
54: |---|---|
55: | stone/imp | the stone wins against scanners and the imps secure ties against papers |
56: | paper/imp | papers that also launch imps |
57: | qscan → body | a quick-scan opening followed by any of the above |
58: 
59: ## Practical techniques
60: 
61: - **Boot.** Copy the working code far from where it was loaded, often leaving a decoy
62:   behind, so that opponents aiming at the start position hit the wrong place.
63: - **Decoys.** Cells that look like code, to waste a scanner's time.
64: - **Step choice.** Steps are usually chosen so the bombing or scanning pattern covers
65:   the core evenly, and so that the warrior does not hit itself before the pass ends.
66: - **Testing.** Strength is relative: a warrior is only as good as the set of opponents
67:   it was tested against.
68:   - Test against a varied set.
69:   - Use random start positions (pMARS without `-f`, or with different `-F` offsets).
70:   - Do not trust differences that are smaller than the noise between runs.

(End of file - total 70 lines)
</content>

5:   python3 tools/spar.py my.red --rounds 300 --opponents s01 s04
6:   python3 tools/spar.py --submit my.red          # set the final submission
7:   python3 tools/spar.py --status
8: 
9: The server address comes from $COREWAR_MCP_URL (default http://arena:8000/mcp).
10: """

12: import asyncio
13: import os
14: import sys

16: from mcp import ClientSession

18: 
19: URL = os.environ.get("COREWAR_MCP_URL", "http://arena:8000/mcp")
20: 
21: 
22: async def call(tool, args):
23:     async with streamablehttp_client(URL) as (r, w, _):
24:         async with ClientSession(r, w) as s:
25:             await s.initialize()
26:             res = await s.call_tool(tool, args)
27:             return "\n".join(c.text for c in res.content if hasattr(c, "text"))

399: P-SPACE
400:        Originating  from  discussions  on  rec.games.corewar,  P-space  is  an
401:        attempt at making warriors more "intelligent" by giving them a  memory.
402:        P-space,  short  for "private", "permanent" or "priviledged" space is a
403:        memory area separate from core whose contents is  not  cleared  between
404:        rounds.  Every  warrior  has  its own P-space for gathering information
405:        about the opposing warrior, but there is a  provision  for  sharing  P-
406:        space in team play (see below).
407: 
408:        P-space  cells contain values in the range 0..CORESIZE-1. The number of
409:        P-space cells can be adjusted with  the  -S  command  line  option;  by
410:        default,  P-space  size is 1/16th of CORESIZE. This number is available
411:        to warriors as the predefined variable PSPACESIZE.   pMARS  updates  P-
412:        space cell 0 at the beginning of each round with the result of the pre-
413:        vious round: 0 signifies a loss in the previous round, a number  larger
414:        than  zero  means that the warrior survived until the end of the round,
415:        the value indicating the number of surviving warriors. That is, a value
416:        of "1" means that the warrior survived by itself (a "win" in a two-war-
417:        rior battle), a value of "2" that two warriors lasted until the end  (a
418:        "tie"  in a two warrior battle), etc..  In the first round, P-cell 0 is
419:        set to -1 (actually CORESIZE-1) to indicate that there is  no  previous
420:        result.
421: 
422:        There are two new instructions for accessing P-space:
423: 
424:        LDP    (Load P-space) loads P-space cell specified by A-value into core
425:               at B-address.
426: 
427:        STP    (Store P-space) stores A-value into P-space cell specified by B-
428:               value.
429: 
430:        It is important to note that P-space cells are refered to by A/B-values
431:        as opposed to A/B-addresses. As an example, "STP #9,#1" stores number 9
432:        in P-cell 1.
433: 
434:        Since  all  P-space access is only via these two instructions, it takes
435:        too much time and space to use P-space for working variables where they
436:        would  be safe from the opposing warrior. P-space was made deliberately
437:        hard to access, unlike a set of general purpose registers.
438: 
439:        P-space can also be used for communication between  warriors  belonging
440:        to  a  team  in multi-warrior core war. To allow communication, P-space
441:        has to be declared as "shared".  You  do  this  by  including  the  PIN
442:        pseudo-opcode in your source:
443: 
444:        PIN    (P-space Identification Number) has a single numerical argument.
445:               If two or more participating warriors have the  same  PIN  argu-
446:               ment,  they  share the same P-space. If the PIN pseudo-opcode is
447:               missing from a warrior's source, its P-space  is  strictly  pri-
448:               vate.  The  PIN  argument  is  not normalized to [0..CORESIZE-1]
449:               before comparison. "PIN 0" and "PIN CORESIZE" are therefore  not
450:               the same.
451: 
452:        P-cell  #0 holding the result of the last round is exempt from sharing,
453:        i.e.  every warrior has its own last round cell even though the rest of
454:        its P-space may be shared.

456: CDB DEBUGGER
457:        Cdb is a line-oriented debugger. It is invoked either by specifying the
458:        -e option (enter cdb immediately), by including debugging  commands  in
459:        the  warrior  source,  or by hitting Ctrl-C during the simulation.  The
460:        debugger is also entered whenever a warrior terminates  ("post-mortem")
461:        if execution was started with the go command.  cdb is very powerful and
462:        has an overwhelming number of commands. You may want to start with only
463:        the most often used commands: step (single step execution), go (execute
464:        until breakpoint), list (look at core),  trace  and  untrace  (set  and
465:        remove breakpoints), and go on to more complex ones later.
466: 
467:        The following commands are available at the cdb prompt; commands can be
468:        abbreviated to the first unambiguous substring.
469: 
470:        <Enter>
471:               repeats the last command issued at the cdb prompt.
472: 
473:        help   displays a brief command summary.
474: 
475:        progress
476:               displays the status of the current game in progress.
477: 
478:        registers
479:               displays the current state of the simulator,  including  program
480:               counters and task queues.
481: 
482:        go     runs  the  simulator until an instruction whose trace bit is set
483:               is executed. If there are no traced instructions go  returns  to
484:               the post-mortem debugger.
485: 
486:        step   executes  the  next instruction in the task queue and returns to
487:               the cdb prompt.
488: 
489:        continue
490:               returns to the simulator to complete the game without  interrup-
491:               tions.
492: 
493:        thread is  similar  to step except that only the current task thread is
494:               traced.
495: 
496:        skip [count]
497:               executes the next [count] instructions  in  the  queue  silently
498:               before returning to the cdb prompt.
499: 
500:        execute [address]
501:               resets  the  task  queue of the current warrior to [address] and
502:               executes it. This is useful in conjunction with edit.
503: 
504:        quit   aborts pMARS and returns to the OS prompt.
505: 
506:        trace [range]
507:               sets the trace bit of the specified address or address range.
508: 
509:        untrace [range]
510:               clears the trace bit of the specified address or address range.
511: 
512:        moveable on|off
513:               specifies whether the trace bit is copied by the MOV.I  instruc-
514:               tion. The default is on.
515: 
516:        list [range]
517:               displays  the specified range of core addresses, a set trace bit
518:               is indicated by 'T'.  Unmodified addresses (DAT.F 0,0) are shown
519:               as blank.
520: 
521:        edit [range]
522:               allows  modifying  core.  The  specified addresses are edited by
523:               typing in new instructions. Typing one or more spaces leaves the
524:               core  address  unchanged, just hitting <return> repeats the last
525:               input, and a syntax error aborts the edit. The full Redcode syn-
526:               tax including labels and (multi-line) EQUates can be used. Label
527:               and EQUate definitions remain in effect until the program termi-
528:               nates.   The  edit  command is useful for modifying warriors and
529:               trying out  single  instructions  without  having  to  exit  and
530:               restart pMARS.
531: 
532:        fill [range]
533:               is  similar  to  edit.   Instructions in the specified range are
534:               replaced by one typed in instruction. Entering DAT.F  0,0  ,e.g.
535:               clears the address range.
536: 
537:        search [pattern]
538:               searches  core  instructions  for  a text pattern in the forward
539:               direction. The next instruction matching [pattern] is displayed.
540:               The  search includes the address number and trace symbol (T), is
541:               case- and space-insensitive and may contain wildcards: * (aster-
542:               iks) matches any number of characters; ? (question mark) matches
543:               exactly one character. E.g. "search ,"  searches  for  the  next
544:               non-blank  address; "search dat*, ?0t" searches for the next DAT
545:               instruction that is traced  and  has  a  zero  B-operand  value,
546:               regardless of modifier, A-operand and B-mode.
547: 
548:        write [file]
549:               opens  a  file for logging subsequent cdb output to. The logfile
550:               is closed by issuing write without an argument.
551: 
552:        echo [string]
553:               is used mostly inside macros. [string] is echoed to  the  screen
554:               followed by <newline>.
555: 
556:        remark [string]
557:               is ignored by cdb and can therefore be used to comment macros.
558: 
559:        cls    clears  the  screen.  The  no-display  UNIX version does this by
560:               echoing an ANSI escape sequence; if this doesn't work  for  you,
561:               you  need to change the CLRSCR string in config.h and recompile.
562:               clear is a synonym for cls .
563: 
564:        display clear|on|off|nnn
565:               (available in display versions only) allows  clearing  the  core
566:               display  (display  clear) or changing the display mode.  display
567:               on changes the display to the default mode, display off (same as
568:               display  0  )  suspends  all  display updates, and display nnn ,
569:               where nnn is a 1 to 3-digit number, sets  the  display  to  this
570:               mode.  "nnn" is interpreted like the parameter to the -v command
571:               line option (see APPENDIX).
572: 
573:        switch [1|2]
574:               (available in display versions only) makes the left (1) or right
575:               (2)  panel  the  current  panel for cdb output. Without a number
576:               argument switch changes to the other panel. If the  right  panel
577:               doesn't exist (initially, or after close, see below), it is cre-
578:               ated first.
579: 
580:        close  (available in display versions only) closes the right cdb  panel
581:               (if it exists) and makes the left panel fullscreen.
582: 
583:        calc expr1[,expr2]
584:               is  a  command  line  calculator. Since calc has no side-effects
585:               other than echoing the result of expression 1 (and expression  2
586:               if  provided).  In  the context of cdb macros it is also used to
587:               assign values to the register variables 'c' through 'z'.
588: 
589:        macro [name][,file]
590:               loads, executes or lists macros. A macro expands to one line  of
591:               cdb  commands  separated by the tilde character (~) (a so-called
592:               command chain, see below).  The command macro name executes  the
593:               macro  "name";  if  "name"  is left out, all currently available
594:               macros are listed.  macro name,file loads macro definitions from
595:               file "file" and executes macro "name"; again, if "name" is miss-
596:               ing, only a listing is produced. Macro definitions are  appended
597:               to the list of previously loaded definitions or replace a previ-
598:               ously loaded macro definition with the same  name.  If  you  are
599:               trying to execute or list macros, but no macros have been loaded
600:               yet, the default macro file "pmars.mac" is loaded automatically.
601:               The  special  macro  file "user" can be specified to input macro
602:               definitions directly from the keyboard. Macro  definitions  con-
603:               sist  of a macro name, followed by the equal sign, followed by a
604:               command (chain).  The macro name can consist  of  any  printable
605:               character  excluding  <space>  and comma; the equal sign is only
606:               allowed at the end of a macro name.  Individual macro lines have
607:               a  limit  of  80 characters, but macro calls inside macro expan-
608:               sions are allowed.  Cdb can hold up to  200  macros  in  memory.
609:               See also the section on cdb macro programming below.
610: 
611:        if <expression>
612:               controls  execution  of commands in macros or command chains. If
613:               <expression> evaluates  to  zero,  the  next  command  block  is
614:               skipped.  A command block consists of either a single command or
615:               any number of commands bracketed by !!  (loop  start)  and  ![e]
616:               (loop  end,  see  section on macro programming below).  <expres-
617:               sion> may contain C-style comparison and boolean operators  (see
618:               below).  An if immediately preceeding a loop end (![e]) can skip
619:               out of the loop.
620: 
621:        reset  is used inside macros in conjunction with if to terminate  macro
622:               execution,    e.g.    inside    an    infinite    loop   (...~if
623:               A==0~reset~...~!).
624: 
625:        pqueue [1|2|..|off]
626:               switches cdb into "process queue mode". In this mode, list, edit
627:               and fill operate on the process queue instead of the core array,
628:               i.e. you can view and modify the process queue as easily as  the
629:               core  array. This is especially useful for debugging complicated
630:               multi-process  warriors.   pqueue  without  argument  uses   the
631:               process queue of the current warrior. With argument 1,2,.., uses
632:               the process queue of warrior 1,2,.., respectively.   pqueue  off
633:               returns to normal mode.
634: 
635:        wqueue [off]
636:               stands for "warrior queue" and is similar to pqueue, except that
637:               numbers provided as arguments for list, edit and fill now  refer
638:               to  warriors:  "list 0" now shows the program counter of warrior
639:               1, "list 1" that of warrior 2 and so on.  wqueue off returns  to
640:               normal "address mode".
641: 
642:        pspace [1|2|..|off]
643:               complements the pqueue and wqueue commands. If a number is spec-
644:               ified, the P-space of that warrior is selected for viewing/edit-
645:               ing. Without an argument, the P-space of the currently executing
646:               warrior is selected. "pspace off" returns to core mode.
647: 
648:        go, step, continue and thread may have a single address  argument.  The
649:        program  counter  of  the current warrior is set to this address before
650:        execution continues.
651: 
652:        The range argument of the list, trace, etc.  commands  has  the  format
653:        <start>,<stop>.  Addresses <start> and <stop> are numbers, special sym-
654:        bols or C-style  expressions  including  special  symbols.   If  either
655:        <start>  or  <stop> is omitted, it defaults to the current address.  If
656:        both are omitted, the range of the last cdb command is used.  A  single
657:        address (without the comma) acts on only that address. Addresses start-
658:        ing with a + or - are interpreted relative to the current address.
659: 
660:        Expressions may contain the arithmetic  operators  -,+,*,/,%  (modulo),
661:        the  comparison  operators ==, !=, <=, >=, and the boolean operators &&
662:        (AND), || (OR), and ! (negation).  Expressions may also include  regis-
663:        ter  variables  C  through  Z  and  the assignment operator =. Operator
664:        precedence is like that of the C-language  and  may  be  overridden  by
665:        parentheses.  Assignment,  comparison and boolean operations are mostly
666:        used with calc and if commands in macros, but can also be used in  Red-
667:        code operands.
668: 
669:        Special address symbols used in cdb commands:
670: 
671:         .     (dot) is the current address (displayed last).
672:         $     (dollar) is the last core address.
673:         A     is the A value of the current instruction.
674:         B     is the B value of the current instruction.
675:         PC    is the program counter of the currently executing warrior.
676:         PC1   is the program counter of warrior 1.
677:         PC2   is the program counter of warrior 2.
678:         LINES is the number of lines available to the cdb display
679:         CYCLE is the current execution cycle (counted down)
680: 
681:        In  process  queue  (pq),  warrior  queue (wq) or pspace (ps) mode (see
682:        pqueue, wqueue, pspace), most of these symbols have a  different  mean-
683:        ing:
684: 
685:         .     (dot) is the current process number (pq),
686:               warrior (wq), or P-space cell (ps) which was displayed last.
687:         $     (dollar) is the last process in the process queue (pq),
688:               the last warrior (wq), or the last P-space cell (ps).
689:         A     is the A value of the instruction of the current process (pq),
690:               the next executing process of the current warrior (wq), or
691:               the P-space selector (ps, same as warrior number if unshared).
692:         B     is the B value of the instruction of the current process (pq),
693:               the next executing process of the current warrior (wq), or
694:               the P-space selector (ps).
695:         PC    is 0.
696:         PC1.. are 0
697: 
698:        Preceding  a  command with the character '@' (ampersand)  will suppress
699:        its screen output, but not output to a logfile.   Preceding  a  command
700:        with  '&' will suppress both screen and logfile output, which is useful
701:        if you are only interested in the "side-effects" of a command.   Start-
702:        ing  a  command  with  a  <Space> character suppresses saving it to the
703:        "last-command" buffer that is recalled by <Enter>.
704: 
705: COMMAND CHAINS AND MACRO PROGRAMMING
706:        Several commands can be issued on one line when separated by the  tilde
707:        character  (~).  These  "command  chains" are useful for repeating long
708:        command sequences, since <Enter> recalls  the  entire  chain  (see  the
709:        examples  below).   Commands  requiring user intervaention (list, edit,
710:        fill) also read their input from the chain.
711: 
712:        The "empty command" (two consecutive tildes or a tilde at  the  end  of
713:        the chain) repeats the last command in the chain.  A command consisting
714:        of <Space> is a null command and is used to simulate  pressing  <Enter>
715:        in list, edit and fill.
716: 
717:        The  exclamation mark (!) character is a special "chain repetitor" com-
718:        mand. The optional expression following '!' specifies  how  many  times
719:        the command chain starting at the beginning of the line or the last '!'
720:        is executed. '!' without an expression repeats until the program termi-
721:        nates.
722: 
723:        The  symbol '!!' is used for nested loops and marks the start of a com-
724:        mand block to be repeated. The command block is  closed  by  '![expres-
725:        sion]'  and  may  contain other command blocks. A command block immedi-
726:        ately following an if command is executed  only  if  the  condition  is
727:        true.
728: 
729:        With  loops,  subroutines  (macros  calling  macros), variables (C..Z),
730:        expressions involving comparisons and boolean  operations,  and  condi-
731:        tional  execution  (if),  the  cdb command language can be used to con-
732:        struct complicated macros for e.g. executing a warrior until a  certain
733:        core  address  has  changed, controlling the 2-panel display, automati-
734:        cally finding the right constants for a  warrior,  etc.  See  the  file
735:        "pmars.mac" for examples.
736: 
737: EXAMPLE CDB COMMANDS
738:        list ,+20
739:               lists the next 20 instructions.
740: 
741:        trace pc-10,pc+10
742:               traces  21  addresses centered around the program counter of the
743:               currently executing warrior.
744: 
745:        untrace 0,$
746:               clears all trace bits.
747: 
748:        go   reg   l+a,+b
749:               chains these commands: execute until the next traced address  or
750:               end of round, display the simulator status and list addresses in
751:               the range A-number to B-number of the current instruction.
752: 
753:        @fill0,100 dat.f 0,0
754:               fills addresses 0 through 100 with 'dat.f 0,0', not echoing  the
755:               changed addresses to the screen.
756: 
757:        write trace.log step !
758:               produces  a  continuous  execution trace by repeating step until
759:               pMARS terminates, saving the output to logfile "trace.log".
760: 
761:        @l x=5 !! @ed x~dat x,0 if (x=x+1)<$+1 !
762:               This command chain could be useful for debugging  a  stone-type,
763:               self-modifying  warrior,  which  is  assumed to occupy address 0
764:               through 4 in this example. The command fills  core  starting  at
765:               address  5  with  "dat  5,0", "dat 6,0", a.s.o., so that you can
766:               tell where a bomb which overwrites the  warrior  came  from.  To
767:               save some typing, you can turn this command into a macro (foo=@l
768:               x=5~..). This is how it works, step by step: Assign 5 to  regis-
769:               ter  x  and  make  it the current address (@l x=5). Start a loop
770:               (!!) and change address x to "dat x,0" (@ed x~dat  x,0).  Incre-
771:               ment  x, if x is then smaller than the core size ($+1), continue
772:               looping (if (x=x+1)<$+1~!). The '@' in front  of  the  list  and
773:               edit commands suppresses screen output.
774: 
775:        @s @4 if b<2 || b>=$-3 reset !
776:               This  command  executes a warrior until the B-field of address 4
777:               points to address 0 through 5: Step and make address 4 the  cur-
778:               rent  address  (@s~@4). If the B-field is less than 2 or greater
779:               than or equal to 7996 (CORESIZE-1-3) stop execution,  else  con-
780:               tinue looping (if b<2 || b>=$-3~reset~!).
781: 
782: SOURCE DEBUGGING DIRECTIVES
783:        Trace  bits can also be set by including debugging commands in the war-
784:        rior source. A comment format is used to retain compatibility with sim-
785:        ulators that do not support source-embedded debugging commands.
786: 
787:        ;debug [static/off]
788:               This  command  enables/disables  all  subsequent source-embedded
789:               commands.  It is used for commenting out other source  comments.
790:               ;debug static has the same effect as the command moveable off at
791:               the cdb command prompt.  ;debug is implicitly added in front  of
792:               every  warrior.  The  last  ;debug  or ;debug static encountered
793:               specifies whether the trace bit is copied by a MOV.I instruction
794:               or not.
795: 
796:        ;trace [off]
797:               ;trace  starts  setting  the trace bit with the next instruction
798:               until EOF or a ;trace off command is encountered.
799: 
800:        ;break sets the trace bit of the next instruction.

836: PMARSV
837:        pMARSv is a DOS version of pMARS with a graphical core display. You can
838:        chose between EGA/VGA graphics or text mode with the  -v  command  line
839:        options or by pressing 'v' during the game. The -v option takes a three
840:        digit argument 'xyz'. Digit 'x' specifies the initial display speed and
841:        ranges  from  0  (fastest)  to  7 (slowest). 'y' is the initial display
842:        mode: 0 for text mode, 1 for standard VGA graphics, 2 and 3 for SVGA, 4
843:        and 5 for EGA, and 6 for CGA graphics.
844: 
845:        The display level 'z' specifies how much is displayed:
846: 
847:        0      Display  nothing.  This  greatly speeds up execution, especially
848:               when in graphics mode.
849: 
850:        1      Display execution of addresses. In text mode,  a  black  '0'  on
851:               blue background is shown for warrior 1, a black '1' on green for
852:               warrior 2, a.s.o.. Numbers blink in white when a DAT instruction
853:               is  executed. In graphics mode, a blue square represents warrior
854:               1, a green square warrior 2, a.s.o.. These colors are also  used
855:               for other core accesses.
856: 
857:        2      Also  display write accesses. In text mode, they appear as dots;
858:               in graphics mode, they appear as two pixels, offset diagonally.
859: 
860:        3      Also display decrements and increments. They are  shown  as  '+'
861:               and '-' in text mode and as two pixels offset vertically or hor-
862:               izontally in graphics mode.
863: 
864:        4      Also display read accesses, which appear as small dots  in  text
865:               mode and as single pixels in graphics mode.
866: 
867:        The  more  is  displayed, the slower runs the simulation.  The argument
868:        for -v defaults to 103, i.e. speed=1, mode=text, level=3.
869:
